articles.title: MacBook Ultra's New Design Won't Stay Exclusive for Long
articles.subtitle: The touchscreen and the OLED panel have dominated discussion about Apple's next high-end laptop, but the redesign wrapped around them may prove to be an equally consequential change, largely because it is not expected to stay unique to the machine for long.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
The touchscreen and the OLED panel have dominated discussion about Apple's next high-end laptop, but the redesign wrapped around them may prove to be an equally consequential change, largely because it is not expected to stay unique to the machine for long.

Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman last week laid out Apple's plan to refresh every Mac it sells over the next two years. In the report, he mentioned that the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro due in 2027, reportedly code-named K104, is said to resemble the design of the high-end K114 and K116 machines while using a standard M7 chip. The design debuting on the rumored " MacBook Ultra " would therefore reach a considerably cheaper Mac within roughly a year of launch, a pattern first reported at the start of July.

Apple last redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2021 alongside the introduction of the M1 Pro and M1 Max chips, and that overhaul ran in the opposite direction to this one. The machine grew thicker and heavier, and Apple restored the HDMI port, the SD card slot, and MagSafe charging that it had stripped out in the preceding generation. Five years on, the company is apparently trying to reverse the thickness.

The chassis is expected to be noticeably thinner and lighter. Swapping a mini-LED backlight for a hybrid OLED stack removes an entire physical layer from the lid, since ‌OLED‌ pixels emit their own light. There has so far been no indication that Apple intends to sacrifice ports to find the rest of the millimeters, which is just as well given how poorly that went last time.

The front of the machine is where the change should be most obvious. The notch is expected to disappear in favor of a much smaller hole-punch camera, a change first indicated on a roadmap from research firm Omdia and since corroborated by Bloomberg. The cutout is said to be pill-shaped, paving the way for an interactive Dynamic Island that expands contextually in the way it does on the iPhone.

Whether the screens themselves will grow is less settled. Omdia claimed that Samsung Display will supply 14.3-inch and 16.3-inch panels, marginally larger than the 14.2-inch and 16.2-inch displays on current models, which would imply slimmer bezels wrapped around a slightly bigger screen. A February report from Bloomberg, however, indicated that screen sizes were not expected to change, but that rumor may not have accounted for a slight reduction in bezels.

Apple is said to be fitting a reinforced hinge so the display does not wobble when tapped, but it is not clear if this will result in any external visual changes. Gurman described the approach to touch as " touch-friendly, not touch-first."

What will become of the high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ is still a loose thread. Gurman's roadmap lists a high-end 14-inch and 16-inch "MacBook" without the Pro suffix, and no separate high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ sits alongside it, though that phrasing is hard to lean on when the exact branding itself is unresolved. The new MacBook "Ultra" could replace the current M5 Pro and M5 Max models outright at a higher price point or arrive above them as a genuinely new tier while they stay on sale.

If the high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ gains Apple's next-generation M7 Pro and M7 Max chips in late 2027, considering that the entry-level M7 model will gain the MacBook Ultra 's design in the first half of that year, it seems inevitable that the high-end machines will follow, meaning that all five of Apple's most powerful laptops will share the same overall design.

articles.title: One last time, this is Tim: Final transcript of Apple’s Q3 2026 earnings call
articles.subtitle: Tim Cook signals for victory! For the 90th and final time, Apple CEO Tim Cook hopped on a conference call with financial-industry analysts to detail the quarter gone by, give a peek at what’s to come, and maybe take one final victory lap.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the 90th and final time, Apple CEO Tim Cook hopped on a conference call with financial-industry analysts to detail the quarter gone by, give a peek at what’s to come, and maybe take one final victory lap. CFO Kevan Parekh and incoming CEO John Ternus were there, too.

This is Six Colors’s complete transcript of the call for July 30, 2026.

Tim Cook’s introduction

Thank you, Suhasini. Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for joining the call. Today, Apple is pleased to report $109.4 billion in revenue, up 16% from a year ago and a June quarter record. We were able to achieve this despite supply constraints and sequential foreign exchange headwinds.

We continue to see enormous customer enthusiasm for our most popular lineup ever, with iPhone revenue growing 22% from a year ago to reach a June quarter record. We saw so much excitement around the best Mac lineup we’ve ever had, growing a strong 29% to achieve a June quarter revenue record. Services also set a June quarter record with $30.7 billion in revenue.

We achieved June quarter revenue records in every geographic segment. We were pleased to see strength across the board with June quarter records in the U.S., Latin America, Western Europe, India, China mainland, Japan, and Southeast Asia. We also achieved June quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets and saw double-digit growth in most emerging markets.

This year’s WWDC was a wonderful showcase of our latest innovations. We were tremendously excited to unveil the all-new Siri AI, a completely reimagined version of Siri that is profoundly capable, deeply personal, and integrated seamlessly across our platforms. And we’ve been absolutely thrilled by the response who’ve been using Siri AI in the developer and public betas.

The reviews from early users have been phenomenal, and it’s been so wonderful to hear from people who are excited about the capabilities we’ve built. And it underscores our philosophy that building AI that is private and based on personal context can change how users find information and get things done with our products in a way that truly enriches their lives.

We really couldn’t be more excited about it, and we are feeling incredibly enthusiastic about the impact it’s going to have.

At WWDC we also announced new tools to help parents keep kids safe online and we were pleased by the overwhelmingly positive reaction. New child safety features like Ask to Browse and Time Allowances will help parents encourage kids to develop healthy digital habits. These new tools integrate guidance from leading clinical and child development research, including the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Our goal is to make it easier for parents to manage what their children see, who they interact with, and how and when they can use their devices. We’re looking forward to bringing these new capabilities to users this fall, in addition to amazing new updates across our operating systems.

Now let me turn to the results for the quarter, beginning with iPhone. iPhone revenue for the June quarter was $54. 3 billion, up 22% from a year ago. We achieved June quarter records in every geographic segment, and set a June quarter record for upgraders. According to IDC, we gained share globally during the quarter. As I’ve said before, this is the most powerful and most popular iPhone lineup we’ve ever had.

More people are relying on iPhone every day for AI, powered by the outstanding performance of A19 and A19 Pro. Across the lineup, iPhone continues to deliver the performance, battery life, durability, and camera capabilities that people count on every day.

Whether it’s the extraordinary camera system of iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, the remarkably thin design of iPhone Air, the balanced performance and durability of iPhone 17, or the exceptional value of iPhone 17E, there’s an iPhone for every customer.

Mac delivered its best June quarter yet, with $10. 4 billion in revenue, growing an impressive 29% from a year ago despite significant supply constraints. This revenue growth was driven by the incredible strength of our latest lineup, with MacBook Pro and the all-new MacBook Neo. According to IDC, we gained share globally.

We also set a June quarter revenue record in developed markets and an all-time record in emerging markets with particular strength in Greater China, where we had an all-time revenue record. In addition, we achieved all-time records for upgraders and customers new to Mac.

With the power of Apple Silicon, the Mac lineup delivers outstanding power-efficient performance, massive memory bandwidth, and next-level AI capabilities. Mac continues to be the ultimate AI powerhouse, excelling at high throughput, on-device inference, and creation across a broad range of AI workloads. And we’re seeing customers increasingly put those capabilities to work, from using Mac Mini as a powerful platform for agentic AI to deploying clusters of Mac Studio systems to run frontier-class models locally.

Across the lineup, customers continue to embrace the Mac family. MacBook Neo has been especially popular, with its distinct design and excellent value resonating with customers around the world, and we’re continuing to work hard to meet demand. MacBook Air, the world’s most popular laptop, continues to deliver the portability and performance customers love with M5.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

Look, it was the 1990s. Everybody was super into two things: edginess, and caring deeply about the environment. A Dungeons & Dragons setting where the entire world had been turned into a hostile desert wasteland by exploitative sorcerer-kings and a bunch of sinewy warriors with psychic powers and an aversion to pants had to slaughter each other to survive was perfect for the zeitgeist.

Though Dark Sun was briefly brought back as part of D&D's 4th edition, a revival for the current 5th edition has been in demand for a while now. Public playtests of the psion, a class first created for Dark Sun, have kept the rumor mill churning, and at Gen Con's D&D keynote Wizards of the Coast finally pressed the big red button that said "dark fantasy nostalgia for '90s kids" and announced its return.

Dark Sun will be getting a rulebook aimed at players called Blood and Power with the psion class in it, as well as a setting guide aimed at Dungeon Masters called Edge of Oblivion. A special printing of the Player's Handbook with Dark Sun's distinctive gore-soaked Wrestlemania art is also planned. All three are scheduled for release next year.

Apparently the lawyers at Wizards of the Coast insisted these books had to be shrinkwrapped because they contain mature content "rated 18+ for profanity and depiction of bloodshed, nudity, and sexuality." I suspect my YouTube feed is about to fill up with videos about how Dark Sun has been ruined by being toned down "because of woke" regardless, but based on the brutal animated trailer above it seems every bit as edgy as it did when I was a kid.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

articles.subtitle: Apple is expecting supply constraints to have a much bigger impact on revenue during the September quarter, Apple CEO Tim Cook said today during Apple's earnings call for the third quarter of 2026. Supply constraints will impact the iPhone, iPad, and Mac.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
We continue to expect high levels of demand. However, with less flexibility in the supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.

Let me stress again. This isn't a partner or supplier issue... It's an incredibly strong iPhone and Mac product cycle that has really yielded a demand beyond our expectation.

The first is, as you would expect, we have benefited from some carry-in inventory in the September quarter. However, we believe we will see decreasing benefit of this over time beyond the September quarter. The second is we're expecting lower cost on certain non-memory components.

Then if you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory continuing to increase and have an increasing impact on our business. [. . . ] The DRAM market has three suppliers. Obviously, if there were more suppliers, that would be good, and it would help us on the supply side and perhaps the pricing side. And so we're evaluating all options.

Of course, it also comes with a brilliant Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion and XDR, tons of expansion, including Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot, and Wi-Fi 6E. And it all comes wrapped in Apple’s sleek design that’s gorgeous in either silver or space black. We loved this model when we reviewed it and still recommend it even at the higher price.

articles.title: Running Simulators Inside Claude Code for Mac
articles.subtitle: Claude Code has a new simulator button. Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. articles.title: Xbox CEO Lays Out Post-Layoff Priorities For Ambitious Growth After A Terrible Year
articles.subtitle: A new Asha Sharma memo has hit Xbox. In it, the CEO shed light on her core priorities and goals to get Microsoft’s gaming division back to strong growth and profits after another 1,600 of its employees were laid off at the beginning of the month.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
A new Asha Sharma memo has hit Xbox. In it, the CEO shed light on her core priorities and goals to get Microsoft’s gaming division back to strong growth and profits after another 1,600 of its employees were laid off at the beginning of the month. Among other things, the plan calls for Xbox to be halfway to a stated goal of 1 billion users per day. It’s currently at 100 million.

Insight into Sharma’s plan comes from The Verge, which shared excerpts from the latest memo to be sent to Xbox staff on July 30. In its earnings report this week, Microsoft reported double-digit declines in revenue on both the hardware and games and services sides, with total revenue for the year declining by $1.7 billion. Xbox’s new CEO laid out four main priorities to pull the platform out of that tailspin in the next fiscal year:

CORE: Strengthen our platform, led by console CONTENT: Grow great games into global franchises CREATION: Make Minecraft the world’s creator platform CONNECTION: Extend the worlds that fans love

CORE: Strengthen our platform, led by console

CONTENT: Grow great games into global franchises

CREATION: Make Minecraft the world’s creator platform

CONNECTION: Extend the worlds that fans love

While each priority begins with the letter C, the actions entailed in following through on them are less obvious. Heading into 2028 and 2029, the plan is to “move into businesses producing meaningful player value and revenue acceleration.” By 2030, the goal is to be “halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins.”

In her now infamous “reset” memo announcing cuts to 3,600 Xbox employees over the next 12 months, including closing or spinning off several studios, Sharma said she wanted Xbox to be one of the few companies that “entertains” more than a billion people each day. Today’s memo stated that Xbox is currently at 100 million. Getting halfway to a billion within four years would seem to require unprecedented growth of nearly 50 percent annually.

Sharma went on to call Xbox “one of the largest stadiums in the world,” a metaphor reminiscent of Google’s failed Stadia play, and said that while the Xbox console remains a “flagship experience,” Xbox will also be searching for new players through PC, cloud, and other platforms.

Long-term plans include monetizing big franchises like Fallout “across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China,” as well plowing even more investment to Candy Crush and Minecraft.

At one point, the CEO reportedly mentioned being more focused on not just the company’s biggest franchises but its “biggest new ideas.” It looks like we’ll have to wait a little longer to find out what those might be.

articles.title: App report: Kicking my World Cup withdrawal
articles.subtitle: (Left to right): Annotate, Kickabout, and Undolly. For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days. But iOS remains a vibrant platform, too, and every now and again, we’ll look at some of the interesting apps being created for iPhones and iPads. This is one of those now and agains.

Want to see your app included in a future round-up? Get in touch at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of your app, and you just might make the cut.

Kickabout

The World Cup is just a memory now, but if you’re missing the daily infusion of soccer (or football, depending on what part of the globe you’re reading this from), Kickabout brings the action back to your iOS device in a very condensed form.

Kickabout will be immediately familiar to anyone who’s ever gathered around a foosball table in a rec room, with a look that will bring a smile to the face of Subbuteo tabletop football aficionados. You take charge of an 8-player team, with players only free to move about certain areas of the pitch. (No length-of-the-field Maradona-esque wonder golazos for your squad.

) You use your finger to drag your players around, swiping any which way to boot the ball toward the goal as you look to rack up the most goals in each 2-minute match.

Goals and shots off the post earn you points, which translates to tickets that you cash in to collect various national teams, from the U.S. all the way to newly minted world champion Spain. You can also buy gear, including stands for your virtual stadium. It’s a fun element that adds to Kickabout’s replayability as you try to assemble your own World Cup field.

Kickabout has both single-player and dual-player modes, though I found the latter to be a little cramped for my iPhone 17 screen. I imagine head-to-head matches are much more enjoyable on the iPad. Still, Kickabout offers plenty of fun even for single players, as you try to master the game’s different difficulty levels.

Kickabout is free to download, and a $3 in-app purchase gets rid of any ads.

Undolly

The Photos app has a built-in tool to weed out duplicate images, but if you find yourself taking a lot of photos, Undolly brings a whole suite of tools that promise to bring order to your iOS device’s photo library. Besides getting rid of duplicates, the mobile app also lists large videos taking up space in your library, rounds up any screenshots you may have stashed somewhere and keeps tabs on other potential space-takers like RAW, timelapse and animated images.

The value of Undolly will depend heavily on how you use your photo library. For instance, I take a lot of screenshots for articles that I don’t always remember to delete, and the app helped me track down some that were three to five years old. I also appreciate Undolly’s swipable comparisons of similar shots, so you can see for yourself whether the images differ enough to keep.

Undolly’s algorithm also rates images by their framing, quality and expressiveness of subject to better help you determine the shots that deserve a place in your library.

While it’s free to download initially, you will have to subscribe to Undolly to use its features, with a free three-day trial letting you get the lay of the land. After that, a monthly subscription costs $4, while annual and lifetime payments go for $15 and $40, respectively.

VWLSS

Nearly five years after Wordle first appeared, we’re still living in a golden age for daily word puzzles. Add VWLSS and its daily serving of mobile word play to the pile, though there are some unique iPhone elements that could help this free offering earn a place in your regular rotation of gameplay.

You have eight words to guess, each tied to a specific category and with all the vowels stripped out. It’s up to you to figure out the actual word, which you can do either by typing in the answer or using a handy speech feature. I prefer talking to typing, though I’m still sore that my guess of “Bob Barker” in the game show hosts category was misheard as “Bob Parker.” Revenge will be mine tomorrow, I guess.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: 10 biggest D&D announcements from Gen Con 2026
articles.subtitle: Wizards of the Coast has firmly established Gen Con as a major annual event for Dungeons & Dragons announcements Related Dungeons & Dragons has officially cemented Gen Con as the premiere event during which Wizards of the Coast will announce each upcoming...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Wizards of the Coast has firmly established Gen Con as a major annual event for Dungeons & Dragons announcements

Related

Dungeons & Dragons has officially cemented Gen Con as the premiere event during which Wizards of the Coast will announce each upcoming year’s slate of TTRPG content. During Thursday night’s D&D Vision Keynote 2027 panel hosted by Baldur’s Gate 3 ’s Theo Solomon, D&D designers and leadership talked about new releases for the game, including updates on new books, digital tools, video games, and collaborations for the next year and more.

Some announcements fill gaps in D&D’s previously announced lineup, including a renewed commitment to publishing full-length adventures. Others revive beloved campaign settings that have gone unsupported for years. The biggest reveal establishes an entire program dedicated to prominent crossovers, starting with a fittingly epic tabletop adaptation of a popular fantasy video game.

Here are the nine biggest D&D announcements from Gen Con 2026.

D&D Icons reunites the game’s most influential creators

Wizards of the Coast is bringing some of D&D’s foundational creators back into the fold through a new initiative called D&D Icons.

“The goal is to bring together legendary creators with the current design team to help shape future content,” franchise creative director Kara Kenna said during a presentation ahead of Gen Con, describing it as “a new initiative that brings together some of the most iconic and influential creators in D&D's history to work on new stories from their unique voice.”

Joe Manganiello will serve as chief creative officer of the initiative, which begins with three pillars of D&D history. Dragonlance creators Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman are also involved, as is R.A. Salvatore, author of the Legend of Drizzt novels.

The program’s first collaborator is Luke Gygax, who will contribute to upcoming Greyhawk material, which includes content drawn from unpublished notes left by his father, D&D co-creator Gary Gygax. “This is just the beginning of this exciting program,” Kenna said. “Who knows who we might bring to the table?”

Third-party studios will make official D&D adventures

D&D has accumulated dozens of campaign settings over its five-decade history, but maintaining all of them has proven impossible for Wizards’ internal team, which will often focus on settings like the Forgotten Realms while others, ironically, remain mostly forgotten. Wizards will enlist prominent third-party publishers to make official D&D books.

“Players shouldn’t have to wait decades before we go back to an Eberron or a Ravenloft or a Dark Sun,” executive producer Greg Bilsland said. “We should be making it easier for everybody to run adventures.”

The first of these partnerships will produce an official Ravenloft book from Ghostfire Gaming in 2027 that incorporates the Domains of Dread recently featured in Ravenloft: The Horrors Within. An Eberron adventure featuring the Lord of Blades will follow in 2028 from Visionary Productions, while Kobold Press will develop new Forgotten Realms material.

These won’t be lightly affiliated supplements published through the Dungeon Masters Guild, which has been the case for quite some time with similar products. They will be official physical and digital D&D releases sold through Wizards of the Coast’s normal distribution channels.

“A big piece of what we’re trying to do here is provide annual support for every one of our settings,” Bilsland said. The exact format may vary between a singular campaign and an adventure anthology, but Wizards’ goal is to provide one major adventure for each supported setting every year in some capacity.

D&D Beyond is getting a major overhaul

Finding a reliable D&D group remains one of the biggest obstacles to actually playing the game. Wizards is trying to address that problem with a new looking-for-group hub at dndbeyond.com/lfg.

articles.subtitle: (Angelo D’Amico/Shutterstock) I’ve been thinking about soap again. Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation: We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been thinking about soap again.

Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation:

We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we usually do. Because I’m me, I started thinking about Apple. Like Apple, the nice hotel’s brand promise is that it’s a nice hotel.

If the hotel didn’t clean its rooms well, didn’t provide soap that smelled nice, didn’t maintain the in-room refrigerator, didn’t clean the swimming pool, it would probably decrease its expenses and increase its profit margin. But over time, it would lose its niceness and become a lousy, overpriced hotel.

Earlier this month, John Gruber wrote about how he hopes incoming Apple CEO John Ternus can perform a bit of a reset on Apple’s advertising strategy. In recent months Apple has announced that it’s adding ads to Apple Maps, and ( as John has documented ) it’s allowed incredibly low-quality, scammy ads to infest Apple News.

While Apple can spin adding ads to Apple Maps as a revolutionary new way for businesses to be discovered, it’s telling that its initial announcement was hidden inside a press release about an entirely different product, and introduced as “Enhanced Discoverability in Apple Maps.

” Those choices show that this isn’t something Apple is actually proud of—and that the people in charge of communicating and explaining Apple’s decisions to the world are at odds with those who are making the decisions about expanding revenue.

Apple also recently expanded App Store ads, creating more clutter at the top of App Store search results. It similarly pitched this as an opportunity for developers—but of course, it’s really an opportunity for developers to take a portion of the money they make from the App Store after Apple’s cut and hand it right back to Apple so that their apps don’t become invisible. What a racket.

But Apple’s approach to grinding out additional revenue doesn’t stop with advertising. The recent release of Apple Creator Studio should’ve been a highlight, because it groups a bunch of useful creative apps in one place for a reasonable price. Instead, its launch was marred by the inclusion of Apple’s free productivity apps in the bundle, requiring users to download new versions and (at least initially) display aggressive subscription promotions in the Numbers, Pages, and Keynote interface.

To this day, you’re confronted with an ad for Creator Studio every time you create a new document in those apps, and their default toolbars contain buttons that won’t work unless you subscribe to the bundle.

As a result, Apple has essentially turned its free productivity suite—software that was designed to enhance the inherent value of Apple’s products—into a freemium package with upsell to a creative professional subscription bundle that’s irrelevant (and a terrible value! ) for most of its existing users.

There are many more examples. Using notifications to promote subscriptions and badging the Settings app to push AppleCare plans are among the ways Apple has chosen to intervene in the user experience to drive revenue.

I’m actually not opposed to the idea that Apple should communicate opportunities for its customers to get more out of their devices—but it should be careful not to cross the line into actively annoying those customers. If someone doesn’t want to see what you offer, you need to accept that and go away—not keep needling them. Apple often falls on the wrong side of that line.

Which brings me back to the hotel soap.

Apple’s most valuable asset is its brand. Not its real estate, not its intellectual property, not even any particular product. Even the mighty iPhone has no value if, over time, the traits that differentiate it from competitor products are erased. Apple’s brand has always stood for higher quality products—you pay more, but you get more. Apple has never wanted to be the low-price leader.

It didn’t put stickers on the first Intel Macs to get some marketing dollars from Intel. It doesn’t load up new Macs with loads of lousy bundled third-party software like so many PCs do.

Those are choices Apple has made that cost the company revenue, but they’ve got a bigger purpose. They reinforce the brand.

Opting not to add more revenue to the bottom line is a difficult choice for anyone working at a profit-driven corporation. I used to be in that position at my former employer, defending the overall product against a constant stream of advertising and biz-dev deal proposals that would add incremental revenue. Believe me, arguing to corporate executives that we should leave money on the table is a deeply uncomfortable role to take on—but it’s vital if you care about the bigger picture.

articles.title: Finishing with Fable 5
articles.subtitle: When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited. Five months later, Fable 5 was released, and I knew it was time to finish Editor, a single-view diffing tool for writers rather than developers.

At MacStories, we all write in Markdown, and we’ve used GitHub to share and sync changes among team members since 2015. GitHub is primarily a developer tool, but it’s a fast, reliable way to share our Markdown-formatted article files, too.

We use GitHub the most for the Club MacStories newsletters. Every week, Federico, Devon, Jonathan, and I work on sections for MacStories Weekly and save them to a GitHub repo. That allows any of us to sync the sections locally for reading, editing, and assembling the issue.

The trouble is that as great as Markdown text editors are to write and GitHub is for versioning and syncing, there isn’t a good way to view the changes someone has made to a document. I know because I’ve been looking for a solution for a long time. Some Markdown apps like iA Writer and Bear support versioning or backups, but I’ve yet to find a text editor that can visualize changes made by someone else based on a document’s Git history.

Of course, developers have many ways to track changes to code, including GitHub Desktop, Kaleidoscope, and Git Tower. Code is just text, so those apps can be used by writers, too. However, the process of writing and editing prose is fundamentally different from code. I’ve tried the apps above and others, and it’s just too hard to track changes in the formats development tools use.

This is what it’s like trying to track changes in GitHub Desktop.

We wouldn’t have stuck with GitHub as long as we have if it didn’t work, but that hasn’t made the friction of reviewing changes any less frustrating, especially on Fridays when we send MacStories Weekly. That’s when I had the idea for Editor. I was trying to parse some changes Devon had made to one of my stories with GitHub Desktop, and the friction finally got to me.

One obvious problem was the side-by-side document view many code diffing tools use. I wanted more detail than most diffing tools offer, but in a single, readable view, so I could skim through changes quickly.

Most agent-assisted projects benefit from some up-front research and planning. I knew what I wanted would sink or swim on the design, not the app’s underlying Markdown viewer, so I spent time researching systems for visualizing document edits.

That’s when I came across Upwelling, a multi-author project from Ink & Switch that describes itself as “an independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.” In their research paper, the authors described my exact problem:

Unfortunately, version control tools like Git, which are designed for software development, do not suit the needs of writers. Git cannot compare or merge files from WYSIWYG editors such as Microsoft Word… and graphical user interfaces for Git are cluttered with complex concepts such as commit hashes and visualizations of non-linear branching and merging histories.

Ink & Switch’s solution, a prototype collaborative text editor, wasn’t what I wanted to build, but the research behind it was full of interesting ideas that helped me settle on several principles for what would become Editor:

Document changes needed to be visible in a single view that carefully balanced highlighting changes with readability;

A writer should be able to instantly switch from the marked-up version of their document to the clean original and edited final version;

Changes needed to be categorized by filterable types like punctuation, word choice, capitalization, insertions, and deletions to reduce clutter in heavily edited documents;

Change types would be color coded using a side rail system inspired by maps of London’s tube system;

Navigating among individual edits needed to be done by simple j/k keyboard input; and

Global document navigation should employ a mini-map of a document’s edit regions (a feature borrowed from developer IDEs like Xcode) to make it easy to jump from one area of a document to another.

Live session held at the Steve Jobs Theater during WWDC26 now available

The Apple Developer YouTube channel shared an interesting 90-minute WWDC26 session today called “ Inside Apple Intelligence and Xcode: Special Presentation. ”

While parts of the presentation can get technical, after all, this is a WWDC session, the video offers very interesting insight into what developers will be able to build using the new technologies, frameworks, and APIs it announced during the event.

Perhaps one of the more interesting parts of the video is a 20-minute segment in which an entire app is built from a single prompt and then further tweaked with follow-up commands.

The result is a WWDC badge tracker app featuring 3D animations, holographic effects, and even Visual Intelligence capabilities—all created from just a few prompts.

Along the way, the demo highlights new Xcode 27 features that come into play before coding begins, including asking clarifying and follow-up questions and mapping out the project in advance.

The session continues with demos and valuable information on how apps can integrate with the new Siri AI, how developers can leverage the new Apple Foundation Models framework, and, in turn, how the framework integrates with the new Core AI framework and the upgraded MLX framework, even when using third-party models.

The special presentation ends with an impressive demo of the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi 2.6 model running locally in LM Studio across four Mac Studios, using the low-latency RDMA-over-Thunderbolt technology Apple introduced with macOS Tahoe 26.2.

articles.title: D&D is getting MTG-style Universes Beyond crossovers starting with World of Warcraft
articles.subtitle: World of Warcraft will be the first in a new line of licensed settings Related Magic: The Gathering brought in $1. 72 billion in annual revenue in fiscal year 2025, and much of its recent success can be attributed to massive sales of its Universes Beyond...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
World of Warcraft will be the first in a new line of licensed settings

Related

Magic: The Gathering brought in $1. 72 billion in annual revenue in fiscal year 2025, and much of its recent success can be attributed to massive sales of its Universes Beyond sets. While some of the game’s most dedicated fans have expressed frustration with the many crossovers, tapping into the fandoms of Final Fantasy, Marvel, and Avatar: The Last Airbender has proved hugely profitable.

Now Wizards of the Coast is extending the strategy to Dungeons & Dragons, kicking off its own version of Universes Beyond with the book Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft.

The 256-page book was announced during Wizards of the Coast’s keynote presentation at Gen Con 2026 on Thursday. It features content from throughout the MMORPG’s 22-year history, including the 2026 expansion, Midnight. The book will introduce 11 new species, like Pandaren and Draenei, along with new elven lineages and pages of lore. Six entirely new subclasses and three updated versions for the D&D 5.

5e ruleset will allow players to become Death Knights, Demon Hunters, Shadow Priests, and more World of Warcraft classes. Players will also have access to more than 60 new spells.

“Our approach in this book is to present all the World of Warcraft classes and each specialization within those classes and tell you how to build that character using either rules in the Player's Handbook or new rules in this book, usually some combination of both,” principal game designer James Wyatt said during a virtual press conference.

Rather than using in-game art, the book draws on a mix of existing art used for previous WoW adaptations like the defunct World of Warcraft Trading Card Game and new illustrations more akin to the style of the Player’s Handbook.

The new book also explores iconic locations from the game, like the Horde capital Orgrimmar and the Lich King’s stronghold Icecrown Citadel, offering stat blocks for heroes and villains like Jaina Proudmoore and Arthas Menethil. Hasbro is also releasing a small line of miniatures, including Arthas and the first Demon Hunter Illidan Stormrage.

An Icecrown Citadel map pack includes access to a digital adventure designed to take a five-person party from level 16 to 20.

Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft includes seven dungeons with 30 bosses and more than 50 new monsters, though fortunately you won’t need to actually gather 10 or 25 people to face any of them. Adapting World of Warcraft to the D&D rules also involved adding some new subsystems, including professions and renown rewards for 23 factions. Players looking for epic loot can find 26 new magic items, including artifacts, plus rules for mounts and companion creatures.

D&D has done smaller crossovers before, releasing box sets based on Rick and Morty and Stranger Things and books based on worlds from Magic: The Gathering. It’s also common for other properties to use the Open Game License to create their own D&D adaptations. White Wolf used the rules of D&D 3.5 to make the World of Warcraft: The Roleplaying Game in 2005, while Free League published The Lord of the Rings Roleplaying with 5th edition rules in 2023.

But embracing Magic ’s Universes Beyond strategy still represents a huge change for D&D. Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft will be released on Nov. 17 and is currently the only confirmed Universes Beyond title, anchoring the Season of Champions in the game’s new seasonal model. But there’s a big hole in the schedule for next summer during the Season of Rebellion.

That name suggests that D&D could be developing something like a Star Wars game, especially since Fantasy Flight’s Star Wars Roleplaying Game was discontinued in 2020.

While Wizards' staff is working on adaptations, the company will also be licensing some of D&D’s iconic settings to other publishers so they can create new adventures.

“Players shouldn’t have to wait decades before we go back to Eberron, Ravenloft, or Dark Sun,” executive producer Greg Bilsland said during the press conference. “We should be making it easier for everybody to run adventures. The problem, of course, is that we have a team that’s only so large, so supporting all those settings with adventure content has been challenging.”

Kobold Press, which created the Horde of the Dragon Queen and The Rise of Tiamat adventures for the launch of 5th Edition in 2014, will be working on the Forgotten Realms. Ghostfire Gaming, which has its own dark fantasy setting, Grim Hollow, will tackle Ravenloft. Visionary Production & Design published Exploring Eberron and Frontiers of Eberron: Quickstone through Dungeon Masters Guild, and it will continue building the setting through this new partnership.

“We're going to continue with the IPs that we've created, like Arcana Unleashed and Dark Sun, and then move forward into a couple of the Universes Beyond, so that we're making sure to balance that and not give too much of one thing,” senior manager of brand publicity and communications Blain Howard said in the press conference. “We had some great learning lessons from our friends across the office doors with Magic: The Gathering on how we can best create Universes Beyond in a meaningful way.”

articles.title: Apple posts record June quarter, but higher costs loom large
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple’s third-quarter 2026 earnings report on Thursday wasn’t your typical financial announcement. It was Apple CEO’s Tim Cook’s last full quarter, which gave it a bit of nostalgia.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
Apple’s third-quarter 2026 earnings report on Thursday wasn’t your typical financial announcement. It was Apple CEO’s Tim Cook’s last full quarter, which gave it a bit of nostalgia. But more importantly, it marked the end of a quarter where Apple announced steep price increases for the Mac, iPad, HomePod, Apple TV, and Apple Vision Pro following increased costs for RAM, storage, and other components.

Turns out that Apple posted its strongest June quarter ever. Apple announced revenue of $109.4 billion for the quarter, a 16 percent year-over-year increase. The company’s gross margin was 50.1 percent, and diluted earnings per share (EPS) were $2.02, up 29 percent year over year.

“Today, Apple is proud to report our strongest June quarter ever, with double-digit revenue growth across iPhone, Mac and Services, and in every geographic segment,” said Cook in a press release. The Mac boasted a 29 percent increase (a June quarter record), and Apple said it set a new all-time record with upgraders and customers new to the Mac. iPhone revenue increased 22 percent, and Services jumped 12 percent.

How the quarter ended year-over-year for Apple:

iPhone: $54.3 billion (up from $45 billion)

iPad: $6.2 billion (down from $6.6 billion)

Mac: $10.4 billion (up from $8 billion)

Wearables, Home, and Accessories: $7.9 billion (up from $7.4 billion)

Services: $30.7 billion (up from $27 billion)

Apple declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share of common stock. The dividend is payable on August 13 to shareholders of record as of the close of business on August 10.

However, there are signs that higher prices affected Apple’s overall earnings in the quarter. For one, the EPS included “a favorable impact of $0.11 from tariff refunds,” meaning the actual price would have been $1.91, a lot closer to the expected $1.88. Furthermore, the all-important Greater China region saw a softening to $18.8 billion versus an expected $19.5 billion, a fairly significant miss. Also, iPad sales are clearly struggling and won’t be helped by dramatically higher prices.

A notable change in Apple’s financial statement is an increase in research and development expenditure. Apple spent $11.7 billion, up from $8.9 billion year over year, a sizable 31 percent increase.

During the call, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh stated that Apple expects revenue to increase between 9 and 11 percent overall for the upcoming quarter and that the current supply-chain shortage will have an effect on Mac, iPhone, and iPad sales. Cook stated that the constraints will have a more severe impact on Apple’s production and that Apple expects to spend more on memory than in the previous two quarters. Apple’s stock was down $23 after the company announced the next quarter outlook

The call was the last for Cook, who is stepping down as CEO in September. During the call, Cook made the following statement:

The transition [to John Ternus as CEO] is going seamlessly, and I am beyond excited for John to step into his new role and lead Apple into its next era. He is truly one of a kind and there is no better person to take the helm of the company.

As I’ve said, I couldn’t be more confident in his leadership, in our executive team, and in the extraordinary people at Apple who are determined to enrich the lives of our users all over the world. We have a bright future ahead, and I truly have never been more optimistic. Apple CEO Tim Cook

articles.title: Snazzy Labs Puts the Mac’s Upcoming Game Porting Toolkit 4 Through Its Paces
articles.subtitle: Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.

Thanks to the upcoming update, Nelson was able to use CrossOver, a Windows-to-Mac compatibility layer that allows PC games to be played on a Mac, to spotlight some impressive numbers on games ranging from Red Dead Redemption to the recently released 007 First Light.

Not all games Nelson tried showed the same leap in performance, but that’s true on compatibility layers like Proton on the Steam Deck, too. What’s remarkable is that it’s all done in software and as Nelson points out, the advent of coding agents like Codex and Claude may help bring more PC games to Mac using the Game Porting Toolkit by reducing the porting costs.

Nelson also makes a pitch for an Apple gaming device. I agree with him that more than ever, the pieces, right down to a hardware-focused incoming CEO, are all there for such a device, and I remain optimistic. However, I’ve made the case for such a device for years now to no avail. Still, whether or not Apple builds gaming hardware itself, watch the full video above. It’s a fantastic view of how far the Mac has come as a potential gaming platform since the advent of Apple silicon.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: D&D Icons brings back legendary creators for Dragonlance, Greyhawk, and Drizzt adventures
articles.subtitle: D&D Icons will deliver authentic new content set in Greyhawk, Dragonlance, the Forgotten Realms, and more Related In a game with 50 years of history, it is inevitable that the creators will come and go.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
D&D Icons will deliver authentic new content set in Greyhawk, Dragonlance, the Forgotten Realms, and more

Related

In a game with 50 years of history, it is inevitable that the creators will come and go. When it comes to Dungeons & Dragons, some names have become so iconic for their contribution to the game and its lore that fans still want to see them involved, no matter how much time has passed. That's exactly the goal of a new product line announced during the D&D Vision Keynote 2027 at Gen Con.

D&D Icons is a new initiative that brings together some of the most iconic and influential creators in D&D's history to work on new stories. The authors involved include Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman, R.A. Salvatore, and Luke Gygax. Actor, producer, writer, and D&D enthusiast Joe Manganiello will serve as chief creative officer for the D&D Icons line. ( Manganiello is also developing his own setting, called Death Saves.)

Weis and Hickman will be working on a Dragonlance TTRPG product for the first time in over 20 years, described in a news release as "the most ambitious Dragonlance volume ever. " R. A. Salvatore will be working under the Icons program to bring back his beloved character, the drow ranger Drizzt Do'Urden from The Legend of Drizzt series.

Finally, Luke Gygax will be working on a Greyhawk project based on unfinished content and unreleased notes left behind by his father, D&D co-creator Gary Gygax. Described as "an adventure through Gary Gygax's eyes," this will be available as early as 2027.

While it's obviously built on a strong dose of nostalgia, this project is presented as forward-thinking. The goal, according to the keynote, is for these legendary creators to work with the current design team to help shape future content. The beloved campaign settings of Dragonlance, Greyhawk, and the Forgotten Realms will keep expanding but without forgetting their history and roots, and by involving the creators who shaped them into what they are today.

Dan Ayoub, head of the D&D franchise at Wizards of the Coast, made it clear when he assumed the role a little over a year ago that one of his priorities was to bring back these iconic creators. He reaffirmed this in a post from last October that featured Manganiello, Weis, and Laura and Tracy Hickman, teasing future projects.

Weis and Hickman's involvement in the D&D Icons line is particularly relevant, as they have a troubled history with Wizards, which includes a 2020 lawsuit. Luke Gygax's presence is also significant, as his father's role in the creation of the game was somewhat overshadowed in recent years by cultural debates and controversies.

Greyhawk needs some new legends

Ayoub's vision for the franchise, encapsulated in the motto "A new dawn for D&D," is clear: to move forward by building on the game's impressive history and foundations. The involvement of beloved creators who carry a lot of goodwill among the community is clearly an important step in that direction, but D&D Icons' promise of shaping the future of the game is what makes it sound most interesting.

articles.author: Daring Fireball
articles.content:
Samuel Axon, Ars Technica:

Apple has released iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and tvOS 26. 6. Apart from potential security hotfixes, these are likely the last updates before the arrival of iOS 27, macOS 27, and so on. articles.title: Unlock or recover your Mac using a special boot volume
articles.subtitle: Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid in Disk Utility, or reinstall Mac OS X or macOS. Over the years, Apple has multiplied those hidden locations and added more sophistication to what they offer.

These boot volumes are:

recoveryOS: The current name and form of the special volume described above, which boots into the Recovery Assistant “app. ” You can run Disk Utility (and First Aid), reinstall macOS, launch Safari to access Apple Support pages, modify startup security settings (rarely required these days), and access Terminal. With Terminal, you can reset your macOS password.

If your Mac can’t start up properly, it will try to launch the Recovery process within recoveryOS, which performs automatic repairs that Apple doesn’t document. If successful, you can then restart into macOS.

Fallback recoveryOS: If recoveryOS is damaged—and that can happen—you can press the power button twice, quickly, and then keep holding it the second time. This fallback recovery volume can’t change startup security, but it can help you diagnose what’s going on. This is the duct-tape belt that helps if your pants come unbuttoned (macOS won’t boot) and your suspenders break (regular recoveryOS fails).

Repair Assistant: From a powered-down state, press the power button until you hear the startup chime, then press and hold Command-D. (On an Intel Mac, hold the D key at startup. ) The Diagnostics app can run hardware tests that might help narrow down a problem before you bring in Apple Support, or they may ask you to boot into that mode and share the results of the tests they have you run.

Repair Assistant can fail, too, if its volume is damaged. You may then have to perform a special “ revive or restore ” operation, which requires another Mac. Or you may need a full reinstall using a bootable macOS installer.

macOS: macOS is a sort of hidden boot volume for the last several releases. You don’t boot from the system; instead, a read-only snapshot of the system is mounted, and then booted from. This is part of Apple making system resources immutable through cryptography and at startup.

Besides using recoveryOS for the above tasks, you might also need to use it to unlock your Mac after locking it in Find My and to reset your password using a FileVault Recovery Key. Here’s how.

Unlock your Mac

While it’s not a common scenario, it could happen to you: you accidentally leave your Mac somewhere, or it’s stolen. Thinking quickly, you launch Find My on another of your devices or go to iCloud. com/find and log in. You then tap or click a few buttons to lock your Mac. If the Mac is connected to the Internet, it restarts and locks immediately.

(Despite promising to display the message you entered when you locked it, macOS does not do so. ) If it’s not connected, it restarts the next time it has Internet access.

The account used to lock the Mac is the only one that can unlock it, and you must be in front of the Mac to perform that operation. Apple limits each Mac to having Find My enabled from a single account. Here are the steps:

When you see the macOS Recovery title, click the account profile below it. Enter the account’s password and click Continue.

If you entered it correctly, “Authentication succeeded” appears. Click Restart.

The Mac restarts and shows Activate Mac after it boots up. This time, all the active macOS accounts are shown. Click one, and then enter its password. Click Next.

You now can choose to either use your Apple Account or a macOS password to continue. If you opt for the Apple Account, enter the full address or phone number as shown. Then enter the account’s password. Otherwise, you can click to enter the Mac password, which Apple says is the last one used to unlock the Mac in a regular session before it was locked.

If you’re the only user on the Mac, that’s easy to figure out. (In testing with Golden Gate public beta 2, I wasn’t able to get the Mac password option to work, and I’ve had it fail in Tahoe, too. ) Sometimes neither works. Choose Restart from the Apple menu in that case and try again.

articles.title: D&D finally goes back to its most hardcore setting with new 'mature' product line
articles.subtitle: D&D is pushing more mature content to cater to all type of players Related It's a new age for Dungeons & Dragons, or at least, that's the message that the game and its parent company, Wizards of the Coast, are pushing after the D&D Vision Keynote 2027 at this...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
D&D is pushing more mature content to cater to all type of players

Related

It's a new age for Dungeons & Dragons, or at least, that's the message that the game and its parent company, Wizards of the Coast, are pushing after the D&D Vision Keynote 2027 at this year's Gen Con. Among the news and exciting announcements that will shape the course of D&D for the next year or more, one stands out as the most hardcore: D&D is going back to Dark Sun, and no punches will be pulled.

Among the many campaign settings created for D&D, Dark Sun and its world of Athos are the most controversial. To get an idea of the vibes, think of Mad Max or, for the old-school anime fans, Fist of the North Star. This is a desolate, post-apocalyptic world where evil has won and heroes mostly fight for survival rather than salvation.

Slavery is also rampant, which is likely one of the reasons why D&D has not returned to the setting since a 4th edition sourcebook was released in 2010. Many fans feared that, if the company ever decided to publish new official Dark Sun products, the gritty, dark fantasy themes and elements of the setting would get sanded down to cater to modern sensibilities. They were wrong.

A short teaser trailer revealed during Gen Con begins with what could only be described as a Mortal Kombat fatality. The abundance of gore, eviscerations, and ultra-violence make it clear that this is a product for adults — if the mature content warning message wasn't enough. The discussion and artwork that were shown to fans also seem to confirm that Athos has not changed. This is still a world devastated by a magical disaster, where immortal sorcerer-kings rule with an iron fist over isolated city states.

Dark Sun will be the centerpiece of D&D's Season of Survival in 2027. Three books will be released: the setting expansion Edge of Oblivion (a campaign sourcebook aimed at Dungeon Masters), the gameplay expansion Blood and Power (which will contain most of the rules and player-focused content), and a limited edition of the 5. 5 edition Player's Handbook featuring dedicated Dark Sun art.

If you thought that the art in the PHB was too fanciful for your tastes, then this is a great chance to give it a gritty upgrade. One of the big new features will be a new character class, the Psion, which will bring psionics back into the game outside of subclasses, specific feats, and a few stray spells.

Image: Wizards of the Coast

The D&D team made it clear that one of their big focuses for the future is to make sure that the game caters to all types of players. The return to Dark Sun signifies that players' requests for more mature content have not been ignored, and it won't end with the world of Athos. At GenCon, actor and newly-appointed CEO of the D&D Icons line, Joe Manganiello, unveiled his homebrew campaign setting, Death Saves.

This is now an official D&D product, inspired by Manganiello's home campaign and his line of clothing. The heavy metal, dark fantasy vibes are quite evident.

There is a lot to be excited about, but as a fan of the original Dark Sun products, I hope that D&D won't simply treat this as an ultra-violent gimmick. The origins of the setting actually harken back to environmental activism: Athos is a grim cautionary tale about the dangers of the unethical exploitation of natural resources and the disasters brought by the unchecked accumulation of power in the hands of the few.
